lesson_title: Interest, Banking and Inflation: the Snowball and the Melting Note
hook_text: R200 under the mattress for ten years. Still says R200. Now worth R123. Nobody touched it.
clip_script: Your money is never standing still — it's either growing or melting. Mrs Adams has R12 000 and two offers, both 6,5%. Simple interest pays R780 a year, every year, forever — it only ever looks at the original R12 000. A straight line. Compound interest is a snowball: year one, 12 000 becomes 12 780. Year two it grows the WHOLE 12 780 — R830,70. Year three, R884,70. After three years the snowball leads by R155. After twenty? Thousands. Same rate, same money — the only difference is what the interest is allowed to touch. Now the villain: inflation. Milk at R32,00 rides the same compound machine at 5% — R33,60, then R35,28. Your R200 note buys six bottles today, five in two years, and after ten years of 5% it keeps about R123 of its power. Cash under the mattress isn't safe — it's melting on schedule. So the rule: money must grow FASTER than prices climb, or it's shrinking in disguise. Earn above inflation, hunt your bank fees, and let the snowball roll.
visual_style: A split screen: a ruler-straight staircase of R780 steps against a snowball rolling and swelling down a hill; a bank statement with fee lines glowing red; a R200 note slowly shrinking beside a milk bottle whose price tag ticks upward.
mood: Streetwise and protective, the voice of someone who checks the interest rate before signing anything.
pacing: Brisk through the two offers, a beat on each year of the snowball, then slow and deliberate as the note melts and the final rule lands.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and put your money on the winning side of the race.
